title: Teaching Cursive
resolution: Resolved: Elementary schools should be required to teach cursive handwriting.
summary: About half the states now require cursive instruction, and more are considering it. Is cursive worth class time in a typing world?

background.p: The Common Core standards adopted by many states around 2010 did not require cursive, and many schools stopped teaching it. Since then, states have added requirements back; by early 2026, Pennsylvania and New Jersey had joined about two dozen other states with cursive mandates, according to Education Next.

Research distinguishes handwriting in general from cursive in particular. A 2023 review by Hewitt and Sachdeva, described in Education Next, found that handwriting (especially for young children) supports letter recognition, spelling and memory better than typing, but found no evidence that cursive offers advantages over printing. Cursive remains useful for reading historical documents and letters written by hand.

disputed.q: Does cursive help children learn more than printing does?
positions: Supporters cite brain and learning research showing benefits of handwriting and argue connected letters add fluency.
A 2023 review found handwriting beats typing for early literacy but no evidence that cursive beats printing.

terms.def: Handwriting in which letters are joined.
Typing skills, taught in many schools in place of or alongside handwriting.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Cursive is a lasting skill that connects students to history and builds fluent handwriting.

args.claim: Cursive lets students read handwritten history.
args.warrant: Letters, diaries, family records and many historical documents are in cursive. A student who can't read it is cut off from primary sources and family history.
args.evidence: National Archives and Library of Congress collections of handwritten documents; Education Next's note that cursive matters for archival research.
args.response: The negative answers that the founding documents are widely available in print, and reading cursive can be taught in a short unit without a full writing requirement.

args.warrant: Forming letters by hand engages memory and attention in ways typing doesn't, helping children recognize letters and spell.
args.evidence: Hewitt and Sachdeva's 2023 review of handwriting versus typing; studies of letter recognition in young children.
args.response: The negative replies that the same review found no advantage for cursive over printing, so the handwriting benefits don't require cursive.

args.claim: Cursive can be faster and more fluent for some writers.
args.warrant: Connected letters let some students write without lifting the pencil, which can help with note-taking and timed writing.
args.evidence: Occupational therapists' and teachers' reports; studies of handwriting speed.
args.response: The negative points out that research found no consistent speed advantage for cursive.

args.claim: A requirement ensures every child gets the chance.
args.warrant: Without a mandate, some schools teach cursive and others don't, so students' skills depend on which school they attend.
args.evidence: State-by-state differences in cursive instruction; parent demand reported in states that passed mandates.
args.response: The negative answers that local schools should decide how to use limited time, and a mandate takes time from other subjects.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Class time is limited; handwriting matters, but cursive in particular doesn't need a state mandate.

args.claim: Cursive's special benefits aren't supported by evidence.
args.warrant: The research supports handwriting over typing, but printing gives the same benefits.
args.evidence: Hewitt and Sachdeva (2023), as described in Education Next: "unlikely that cursive offers more cognitive benefits than printing."
args.response: The affirmative answers that cursive is still handwriting, so it shares those benefits, and it adds the ability to read historical documents.

args.claim: Mandates take time from other subjects.
args.warrant: Every hour spent on cursive practice is an hour not spent on reading, science or history content.
args.evidence: Education Next's opportunity-cost argument; data on elementary instructional time.
args.response: The affirmative replies that a few minutes a day over a year or two is enough, and handwriting practice can be combined with spelling and writing.

args.claim: Signatures and daily life no longer require cursive.
args.warrant: Most signing is electronic, and printed signatures are legally accepted, so cursive isn't needed for adult life.
args.evidence: Laws on electronic signatures; Education Next on signatures.
args.response: The affirmative answers that reading cursive, not just signing, is the main skill at stake.

args.claim: Reading cursive can be taught without a writing mandate.
args.warrant: A short unit can teach students to read cursive for history class, which captures the main benefit at a fraction of the time.
args.evidence: Examples of history and archival programs that teach cursive reading.
args.response: The affirmative replies that learning to write cursive is the most reliable way to learn to read it.

strawmen.strawman: Cursive fans are just nostalgic for the old days.
strawmen.why: Supporters cite reading primary sources and research on handwriting.
strawmen.steelman: Cursive lets students read handwritten history and family records, shares handwriting's learning benefits, and a requirement gives every child the chance to learn it.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents think handwriting doesn't matter at all.
strawmen.why: Many opponents support handwriting; they question cursive specifically.
strawmen.steelman: Handwriting helps early learning, but printing gives the same benefits, so a cursive mandate takes time from other subjects without added gains.

weak.arg: Without cursive, students can't read the Constitution.
weak.why: The Constitution is widely printed in modern type; the stronger point is about handwritten sources generally.
Students write by hand often, and research shows handwriting matters; argue about cursive specifically.
